provenance: Generated corpus. The verdicts are derived expectations.
purpose: Non-regression corpus for replacing DataContractJsonSerializer with CrystalJson.

comparedRuntime.note: DCJS on .NET 10 is not a target. It is captured only to detect DCJS's own drift, and expectedNet10 appears on a case only where it differs.

targetLibrary.name: CrystalJson (SnowBank.Data.Json)
targetLibrary.note: 7.4.3 is tagged, and the Collection<T> defect is fixed in it. Acme pinned SnowBank.Core 7.4.2 through CPM when the corpus was written, where the defect is still live. The repository now develops 7.4.4.

equivalenceCriterion: CLR-binding equality: two documents are equivalent if deserializing both into the same concrete C# type yields the same content. Date syntax, enum representation, key order, whitespace and escaping style are absorbed. null vs empty string, null vs empty collection, [Flags] enum rendering, and date precision/offset are not absorbed.

collection-data-contract-naming.exercises: [CollectionDataContract] with custom ItemName, KeyName and ValueName.
collection-data-contract-naming.wireDelta: These names are ignored in JSON. With ItemName="entry" and KeyName="code"/ValueName="label", the output stays ["x","y"] and [{"Key":...,"Value":...}]. They are XML attributes.
collection-data-contract-naming.notes: 217 occurrences in the application, so 217 attributes with no effect on the JSON path. The port can ignore all of them.

collection-list-and-interfaces.exercises: List<T>, IList<T>, IEnumerable<T>, ICollection<T>, array, nesting. The interface-declared members are the interesting ones: the reader has to choose a concrete type.

collection-non-generic-subclass.exercises: Non-generic subclasses of List<T> and Collection<T>, as a member.
collection-non-generic-subclass.notes: 31 List-derived and 105 Collection-derived. This family crashed on serialization in 7.4.2, fixed in 7.4.3.

collection-of-t-member.exercises: Collection<T> as a member (396 occurrences): the exact shape that deserialized to null with no error on CrystalJson 7.4.2.
collection-of-t-member.notes: Permanent regression witness for the fix shipped in 7.4.3, not a live defect.

collection-subclass-as-root.exercises: The same family as the root type rather than a member. Root and member took different code paths in the 7.4.2 defect, failing loudly in one and silently in the other.

contract-is-reference.exercises: [DataContract(IsReference = true)]: object identity on the wire, an id first and back-references after it.
contract-is-reference.notes: DCJS refuses to serialize an IsReference type to JSON, with "The JSON format does not support references because there is no standardized format for representing references". One occurrence in the whole source tree, so either this type is never serialized to JSON (only XML and WCF), or it is a latent crash. Either way the replacement has nothing to support here. The open question is the intent of the single site: shared identity that must survive a round trip, or an attempt to avoid duplicating an object.
contract-is-reference.expectedError: SerializationException: The type 'Acme.Zoo.Cases.ContractIsReference.SharedNodeDto' cannot be serialized to JSON because its IsReference setting is 'True'. The JSON format does not support references because there is no standardized format for representing references. To enable serialization, disable the IsReference setting on the type or an appropriate parent class of the type.

datetime-minvalue-landmine.exercises: DateTime.MinValue with kind Unspecified or Local: DCJS throws on serialization as soon as the machine sits at a positive UTC offset.
datetime-minvalue-landmine.wireDelta: This case is expected to fail. DateTime.MinValue is the default value of an unassigned DateTime, the application has 343 DateTime members, and EmitDefaultValue defaults to true. So any DTO carrying an unassigned DateTime throws east of Greenwich and works in London. Corollary: a document that omits a non-nullable DateTime member cannot be round-tripped, because the absence becomes MinValue and the rewrite then throws.
datetime-minvalue-landmine.notes: Found while building the corpus, not anticipated. The behavior is identical on net472 and net10.
datetime-minvalue-landmine.expectedError:
SerializationException: DateTime values that are greater than DateTime.MaxValue or smaller than DateTime.MinValue when converted to UTC cannot be serialized to JSON.  ---> ArgumentOutOfRangeException: Specified argument was out of the range of valid values.
Parameter name: value

datetime-minvalue-mitigated.exercises: The same default DateTime, declared the two ways that survive: EmitDefaultValue=false, or nullable. Plus MinValue explicitly in UTC, which serializes.
datetime-minvalue-mitigated.notes: The healthy counterpart of the previous case, so one case is expected to fail and the other to succeed.

diagnostic-double-contract.exercises: A DTO carrying both [DataMember(Name="enabled")] and [JsonProperty(PropertyName="ACTIF")] on the same member.
diagnostic-double-contract.wireDelta: This case is expected to fail loudly rather than to match. 2307 members carry both attributes, and 1726 of those give each attribute a different name. DCJS honors its own attribute and ignores the other, so the output is {"code":..,"enabled":true,"label":..}. Newtonsoft does the reverse. A serializer that understands both attribute families sees both and applies only one, silently.
diagnostic-double-contract.notes: This is an architecture defect, not a compatibility target. The remedy is to split the DTO. The ClientFacingDto and LegacyWireDto types in the same file are the worked example for the guide.

dictionary-non-string-key.exercises: int and Guid keys. A JSON object cannot express them, so the pair array is not a stylistic choice here, it is the only option.
dictionary-non-string-key.wireDelta: The order follows insertion, not sorting: key 2 comes before key 1. Worth keeping in mind for the canonical form.

dictionary-string-key.exercises: Dictionary with string keys, in DCJS's default form: an array of {"Key":...,"Value":...} pairs.
dictionary-string-key.wireDelta: The largest blast radius of the corpus. C# binds the pair array and the object map alike, and no JavaScript client does: obj.map["k"] and obj.map[i].Key are not interchangeable. The read side is worse. DCJS reads the object-map form as an empty dictionary with no error, so the input {"map":{"alpha":"first"}} yields the output {"map":[]}. Silent data loss.
dictionary-string-key.notes: The application never sets UseSimpleDictionaryFormat (0 occurrences), so every map is in the pair-array form.

enum-flags.exercises: [Flags]: combined value, single value, named combination, undeclared bit.
enum-flags.wireDelta: Numeric and string renderings are not equivalent for a flags enum: a client doing x & 4 can do nothing with "Read, Write". DCJS emits 3 for Read|Write, and throws when reading "Read, Write".

enum-plain-and-enum-member.exercises: Enums with and without [EnumMember(Value=)], nullable, in a list, and a numeric value outside the declared set.
enum-plain-and-enum-member.wireDelta: DCJS ignores [EnumMember(Value=)] and emits the number, so stateWithValue is 5 and not "on-loan". On the read side the string form throws. So the 810 [EnumMember] occurrences (76 of them with Value=) have no effect on the JSON path, and a serializer that emits enum strings breaks every remaining DCJS reader. A value outside the declared set (4242) is accepted silently.
enum-plain-and-enum-member.notes: The criterion holds that 5 and "FooBar" are equivalent. That is true at the binding level, and false when the reader on the other side is DCJS.

extensible-data-object.exercises: IExtensibleDataObject: unknown members are retained and re-emitted, including a nested object. This case doubles as the duplicate-key probe.
extensible-data-object.notes: 2 types once generated code is excluded; the other 27 were in a generated WCF proxy, which dies with its generator. The risk itself is general: any read-modify-rewrite of a stored document through a partial or older DTO silently loses the undeclared members. The chosen answer is to stay on the generated proxy (a typed view over the DOM, so nothing is rebuilt) and never to go back through ToValue(), which is the lossy operation. That still has to be verified, and the generator is no longer out of reach: it lives in this repository (SnowBank.Serialization.Json.CodeGen), next to the corpus. No assertion in this case checks the retention of unknown members; the runner only proves the binding. Duplicate-key probe: an unknown member differing from a declared one only by case ("Known" against "known") is kept alongside it, but JSON is case-sensitive, so these are not duplicate keys. The assumption that DCJS never produces a duplicate key survives the probe.

legacy-arraylist-members.exercises: Non-generic ArrayList as a serialized member, with heterogeneous content, an empty one and a null one.
legacy-arraylist-members.notes: 6 member positions in a statistics counter DTO. Added because rc.1 changes how non-generic collections bind: without this case, a re-run would assume rather than verify. Nothing on the wire records the element types, so a reader has only the JSON scalar kinds to work from.

lifecycle-callbacks.wireDelta: The mutation done by OnSerializing is visible in the output, as trace:"start|onSerializing". A serializer that does not run these callbacks returns an object that is structurally correct and semantically wrong, with nothing to signal it.

member-emit-default-false.exercises: EmitDefaultValue=false on every category of default, next to members left at true.
member-emit-default-false.wireDelta: DCJS emits defaults and nulls explicitly, as keptInt:0 and keptList:null. A serializer that omits them by default drops those members. A client doing obj.x.toFixed(2) or obj.items.length then throws a TypeError on undefined, which it did not do before.
member-emit-default-false.notes: 1062 occurrences of EmitDefaultValue=false, against 33 of =true, so the default (true) is almost always implicit.

member-fields-versus-properties.exercises: Fields carrying [DataMember], including a readonly one and a private one, next to properties.

member-ignore-data-member.exercises: [IgnoreDataMember] on an opt-out type (no [DataContract]), the only configuration where the attribute does anything.

member-is-required.exercises: IsRequired=true. The interesting behavior is on the read side: a document missing the member throws a SerializationException instead of taking the default.
member-is-required.notes: Only 11 occurrences, kept because its failure is loud and specified.

member-name-rename.exercises: [DataMember(Name=)]: 5644 of 13883 members (41%). The wire order is ordinal on the effective name.
member-name-rename.wireDelta: Key order only: DCJS sorts by wire name in ordinal order, uppercase first. Absorbed by the criterion.
member-name-rename.notes: The most frequent pattern of the corpus.

member-non-public.exercises: private, internal and protected members carrying [DataMember] do serialize.
member-non-public.notes: 765 non-public members. The visibility must be preserved, or the case stops testing anything.

member-order.exercises: Order= mixed with unordered members. Unordered members come first, then the ordered ones by Order, with ties broken in ordinal order.

member-order-across-inheritance.exercises: Member order in a contract hierarchy: base-type members come before derived-type members, regardless of alphabetical order.

null-versus-empty.exercises: null against empty string, and null collection against empty collection: the two distinctions the equivalence criterion refuses to absorb.
null-versus-empty.wireDelta: The DCJS round trip is not idempotent in shape. The input {"emptyString":""} comes back as {"emptyList":null,"emptyString":"","nullList":null,"nullString":null}: the absent members become explicit nulls. The stored data therefore already drifts toward the explicit form.
null-versus-empty.notes: obj.x.trim() throws on null and works on "". obj.items.length throws on null and is 0 on [].

poco-no-data-contract.exercises: Opt-out mode, with no attribute at all. Public read/write members are emitted, and members with no setter are omitted.
poco-no-data-contract.wireDelta: Wire names in PascalCase (the raw property name), with no renaming.
poco-no-data-contract.notes: The trap is the getter-only member, silently absent.

poly-known-type-abstract.exercises: [KnownType] with an abstract member, a member declared as object, and a polymorphic list. Emission of the __type hint.
poly-known-type-abstract.wireDelta: Key order is not universally irrelevant. DCJS requires __type to be the first property, and the hint placed last fails with MemberAccessException "Cannot create an abstract class". The $type spelling (the System.Text.Json style) fails the same way. The value encodes "TypeName:DataContractNamespace", so a client that switches on __type breaks if the spelling changes.
poly-known-type-abstract.notes: 1146 [KnownType] occurrences. This is the one exception to key-order irrelevance.

poly-serializer-known-types.exercises: Known types passed through the constructor instead of declared by attribute.
poly-serializer-known-types.notes: The application's whole serializer configuration surface comes in two forms: 55 call sites use the type-only constructor, 4 use type plus knownTypes. There is no DataContractJsonSerializerSettings, no surrogate, no DataContractResolver, no UseSimpleDictionaryFormat and no EmitTypeInformation in the entire source tree. So the netfxOnly part of the corpus is empty.

primitive-datetime-kinds.exercises: Every DateTimeKind the application really stores, plus DateTimeOffset, a nullable one and a sub-second one.
primitive-datetime-kinds.wireDelta: This blocks a mixed deployment. (1) DCJS refuses ISO 8601 on read: the input {"utc":"2026-07-30T12:34:56Z"} throws, so any data written in ISO 8601 is unreadable by the remaining DCJS path. (2) DateTimeOffset comes out as a nested object, {"DateTime":"/Date(..)/","OffsetMinutes":120}, not as a string. (3) Local and Unspecified carry the UTC offset of the machine that serialized them, and an ISO 8601 rendering with no offset is read as local time by a browser, which shifts the computed instant.
primitive-datetime-kinds.notes: Timezone sensitive: the Local and Unspecified members only reproduce in the timezone recorded in the manifest.

primitive-scalars.exercises: Scalar types and values at the edges: int min and max, long above 2^53, double 0.1 / 1e-7 / -0.0, decimal with trailing zeros, Guid, Uri, TimeSpan, byte[], char.
primitive-scalars.wireDelta: Three deltas. (1) byte[] comes out as an array of numbers ([0,1,127,128,255]), not as base64. (2) decimal preserves the scale (1.100, not 1.1), which is money on screen in the accounting module. (3) long above 2^53 comes out as a bare number: exact in C#, silently wrong in a browser. Also: TimeSpan as an ISO 8601 duration (P1DT2H3M4.005S), double in uppercase E notation (1E-07), and -0.0 as -0.

primitive-string-escaping.exercises: Quotes, backslash, '/', control characters, accented Latin, a non-Latin script, right-to-left text, an astral character (a surrogate pair), NFC against NFD, and content that looks like a date.
primitive-string-escaping.wireDelta: Escaping style is absorbed by the criterion. Recorded anyway: DCJS escapes '/' as '\/', emits accented Latin and right-to-left text raw, and escapes the astral character as the pair \ud83d\ude00. A string member whose content looks like a date does come back as a string.
primitive-string-escaping.notes: NFC against NFD: two visually identical texts, different bytes, and therefore different hashes. That matters for the canonical form, and sits outside the serializer's scope.

serializable-with-data-contract.exercises: A type that carries both [DataContract] and ISerializable, with different member names in the two mechanisms so the answer is unambiguous.
serializable-with-data-contract.notes: The combination is impossible: DCJS rejects it when building the contract, with InvalidDataContractException "cannot be ISerializable and have DataContractAttribute". A count by file gave 7 files doing both. Counted by type it is zero, because those files held two distinct types. So in this product the two mechanisms are always carried by different types, and an ISerializable met during the port never has a [DataContract] competing for the wire.
serializable-with-data-contract.expectedError: InvalidDataContractException: Type 'Acme.Zoo.Cases.SerializableWithDataContract.DualContractDto' cannot be ISerializable and have DataContractAttribute attribute.

smoke-minimal.exercises: Two renamed members, nothing else. It validates the generation toolchain itself.
